title: I. At Grushenka’s
paragraphs: Alyosha was heading across the cathedral square to the widow Morozov’s house, to see Grushenka. She had sent Fenya to him early that morning with an urgent message asking him to come. Fenya told him, when he questioned her, that her mistress had been particularly upset since the day before. In the two months since Mitya’s arrest, Alyosha had often visited the widow Morozov’s house, partly because he wished to and partly to carry messages for Mitya. Three days after Mitya was arrested, Grushenka had fallen gravely ill, and she remained ill for almost five weeks. For one whole week she had lain unconscious. She had changed a great deal. She was thinner and a little sallow, although for the last fortnight she had been well enough to go out. Yet to Alyosha her face was more attractive than ever, and he liked meeting her eyes when he came in. Her face had taken on a look of firmness and intelligent purpose. There were signs in her of a spiritual transformation, and one could see a steadfast, fine, humble determination that nothing could shake. A small vertical line had appeared between her brows, and at first glance it gave her charming face a thoughtful, almost stern look. Hardly a trace remained of her old frivolity.

Alyosha found it strange, too, that the poor girl had not yet lost her youthful cheerfulness. A calamity had struck her: she was engaged to a man who was arrested for a terrible crime almost at the very moment of their engagement. She had been ill, and a sentence that seemed all but certain hung over Mitya. Even so, her cheerfulness had survived. Her once proud eyes now had a soft light in them, though now and then they blazed with the old vengeful fire, whenever one troubling thought gripped her harder than ever. What troubled her was the same as always: Katerina Ivanovna, whom Grushenka had even raved about in her delirium. Alyosha knew she was dreadfully jealous of her. And yet Katerina Ivanovna had not visited Mitya in prison even once, though she could have gone whenever she pleased. All this set Alyosha a hard problem, since he was the only person Grushenka confided in, and she kept asking him for advice. Sometimes he had nothing to tell her.

Anxious, he went into her rooms. She was at home. She had returned from visiting Mitya half an hour earlier, and the way she sprang up from her chair to meet him showed Alyosha she had been waiting for him with great impatience. On the table lay a pack of cards, dealt out for a game of “fools.” On the far side of the room a bed had been made up on the leather sofa, and Maximov lay on it, half sitting up. He wore a dressing-gown and a cotton nightcap. He was clearly ill and weak, but he was smiling happily. The homeless old man had come back from Mokroe with Grushenka two months earlier and had simply stayed, and he was still there. He had arrived with her in rain and sleet, sat down on the sofa soaked and frightened, and looked at her without a word, with a timid, imploring smile. Grushenka was in terrible grief and just coming down with fever. In everything she had to do in the first half-hour after she got home, she nearly forgot he was there. Then she happened to glance at him closely, and he gave a pitiful, helpless little laugh. She called Fenya and told her to give him something to eat. All that day he sat in the same spot, hardly moving. When it grew dark and the shutters were shut, Fenya asked her mistress:
“Is the gentleman staying the night, mistress?”
“Yes. Make up a bed for him on the sofa,” Grushenka answered.
She questioned him further and learned that he literally had nowhere to go. “Mr. Kalganov, my benefactor, told me flat out that he would not receive me again, and he gave me five roubles.”

“Well, God bless you, you’d better stay, then,” Grushenka decided, in her grief, and smiled at him with pity. Her smile wrung the old man’s heart, and his lips twitched with grateful tears. So the penniless wanderer had been with her ever since. He didn’t leave the house even while she was ill. Fenya and her grandmother, the cook, did not turn him out. They kept serving him his meals and making up his bed on the sofa. Grushenka had got used to him. When she came home from Mitya (she had started visiting him in prison before she was properly well), she would sit down and chat with “Maximushka” about small matters, so as not to think about her sorrow. The old man proved to be a good teller of stories now and then, and in the end she couldn’t do without him. Besides Alyosha, who did not come every day and never stayed long, Grushenka saw almost nobody. Her old merchant lay gravely ill at this time, “at his last gasp,” as people in town said, and in fact he died a week after Mitya’s trial. Three weeks before he died, sensing the end was near, he had at last made his sons, their wives and their children come upstairs to him, and he commanded them not to leave him again. From then on he gave his servants strict orders not to let Grushenka in, and to tell her, if she came, “The master wishes you long life and happiness and tells you to forget him.” Still, Grushenka sent almost every day to ask after him.

“You’ve come at last!” she cried, dropping the cards and welcoming Alyosha with delight. “Maximushka has been frightening me that you might not come. Ah, how much I need you! Sit down at the table. What will you have? Coffee?”
“Yes, please,” said Alyosha, taking his seat at the table. “I’m very hungry.”

“Good for you. Fenya, Fenya, coffee!” Grushenka cried. “It’s been ready for you for ages. And bring some little pies, and see they’re hot. Do you know, we had a storm over those pies today. I took them to the prison for him, and can you believe it, he threw them back at me. He wouldn’t eat them. He tossed one on the floor and stamped on it. So I told him, ‘I’m leaving them with the warder. If you haven’t eaten them by evening, your venomous spite must be all the food you need!’ And I walked out. Can you believe it, we quarreled again? Every time I go, we quarrel.”
Grushenka said all this in a single breath, upset as she was. Maximov grew nervous, smiled right away and looked down at the floor.
“What was the quarrel about this time?” Alyosha asked.

“I never saw it coming. Just think, he’s jealous of the Pole! ‘Why do you keep him?’ he said. ‘So now you’re keeping him.’ He’s jealous, jealous of me all the time, jealous when he’s eating, jealous when he’s asleep! Last week he even got it into his head to be jealous of Kuzma.”
“But he knew about the Pole already?”

“Yes, he did, but there you are. He has known about him from the very start, and today all at once he jumped up and began raging about him. I’m ashamed to repeat what he said. The silly fellow! Rakitin went in just as I was coming out. Maybe Rakitin is egging him on. What do you think?” she added, as if it hardly mattered.
“He loves you, that’s all it is. He loves you so much. And now he’s especially worried.”

“Well, he might be, with the trial tomorrow. And I went to him to say a word about tomorrow, because I’m afraid to think what will happen then. You say he’s worried, but how worried am I! And he goes on about the Pole! He’s too silly! At least he isn’t jealous of Maximushka yet.”
“My wife was terribly jealous over me, too,” Maximov put in a word.
“Jealous of you?” Grushenka couldn’t help laughing. “Who could she have been jealous of?”
“The servant girls.”

“Hush, Maximushka, I’m not in a laughing mood now. I’m angry. Stop eyeing the pies. You’re not getting any. They’re bad for you, and I won’t give you vodka either. I have to look after him as well, as if I were running an almshouse,” she laughed.
“I don’t deserve your kindness. I’m a worthless creature,” said Maximov, tears in his voice. “You’d do better to spend your kindness on people who are more use than I am.”

“Ech, everybody is of use, Maximushka, and who can say who’s most useful? If only that Pole didn’t exist, Alyosha. He’s gone and fallen ill today, too. I’ve been to see him as well. And I’ll send him some pies, too, on purpose. I hadn’t sent him any, but Mitya accused me of it, so now I will! Ah, here comes Fenya with a letter! Yes, it’s from the Poles—begging again!”

Pan Mussyalovitch had indeed sent a very long letter, eloquent in his usual way, begging her to lend him three roubles. A receipt for the sum was enclosed, with a promise to repay it within three months, signed by Pan Vrublevsky as well. Over the fortnight of her recovery Grushenka had received many such letters from her former lover, each with a receipt like this. She knew, though, that the two Poles had called to ask about her health while she was ill. The first letter they sent her was a long one, written on large notepaper and sealed with a big family crest. It was so obscure and high-flown that Grushenka put it down before she was halfway through, unable to make anything of it. She was in no state to deal with letters then. Next day a second letter followed the first, in which Pan Mussyalovitch asked her for a loan of two thousand roubles, for a very short time. Grushenka left that one unanswered too. Then came a whole series of letters, one a day, all just as pompous and rhetorical, but the sum they asked for kept shrinking. It fell to a hundred roubles, then twenty-five, then ten, and at last Grushenka got a letter in which both Poles begged for only one rouble and enclosed a receipt signed by the two of them.

Then Grushenka suddenly felt sorry for them, and at dusk she went to their lodging herself. She found the two Poles in great poverty, almost starving, with no food or firewood, without even cigarettes, and in debt to their landlady. The two hundred roubles they had carried off from Mitya at Mokroe had soon vanished. But Grushenka was surprised to be received with haughty dignity and self-importance, with the most elaborate manners and pompous speeches. Grushenka simply laughed and gave her old admirer ten roubles. Then she told Mitya about it, laughing, and he wasn’t in the least jealous. But from that day the Poles had fastened on Grushenka and bombarded her daily with demands for money, and she had always sent them small sums. And now, today of all days, Mitya had taken it into his head to be fearfully jealous.

“Like a fool, I stopped by to see him for just a minute on my way to Mitya’s, because he’s ill too, my Pole,” Grushenka began again, in a nervous rush. “I was laughing as I told Mitya about it. ‘Just think,’ I said, ‘my Pole had the happy idea of singing me his old songs, with a guitar. He thought I’d be touched and marry him!’ Mitya jumped up, swearing.... Well, there you are, I’ll send them the pies! Fenya, is it that little girl they’ve sent? Here, give her three roubles, wrap a dozen pies up in paper and tell her to take them. And you, Alyosha, be sure to tell Mitya that I did send them the pies.”
“I wouldn’t tell him that for anything,” said Alyosha with a smile.
“Ech! You think it hurts him? Not a bit. He’s jealous on purpose. He couldn’t care less,” Grushenka said bitterly.
“On purpose?” Alyosha asked.

“You’re silly, Alyosha, I tell you. For all your cleverness you understand nothing about this. It doesn’t offend me that he’s jealous of a girl like me. What would offend me is if he weren’t jealous. That’s the way I am. Jealousy doesn’t insult me. I have a fierce heart too, and I can be jealous myself. What does offend me is that he doesn’t love me at all. I tell you, he’s jealous now _on purpose_. Do you think I’m blind? Can’t I see? Just now he started on about that woman, about Katerina. She was this, she was that, she’d ordered a doctor from Moscow to try to save him, she’d ordered the best lawyer, the most learned one too. So he loves her, if he’ll sing her praises to my face. Shame on him! He’s treated me badly himself, so he went for me first, to make me the guilty one and put it all on me. ‘You were with your Pole before me, so I can’t be blamed over Katerina.’ That’s what it all comes to. He wants to dump the whole blame on me. He picked a quarrel on purpose, on purpose, I tell you, but I’ll—”
Grushenka never got to say what she would do. She hid her eyes in her handkerchief and broke into violent sobs.
“He doesn’t love Katerina Ivanovna,” Alyosha said firmly.

“Well, whether he loves her or not, I’ll find out soon enough,” said Grushenka, her voice turning threatening as she took the handkerchief from her eyes. Her face was twisted. Alyosha saw with sorrow that it had changed from mild and calm to sullen and spiteful.

“Enough of this nonsense,” she said suddenly. “That’s not what I sent for you about. Alyosha, darling, tomorrow—what is going to happen tomorrow? That’s what eats at me! And it eats at no one but me! I look around, and nobody is thinking about it. Nobody cares. Do you even think about it? Tomorrow he’s going on trial, you know. Tell me, how will they try him? You know it was the valet, the valet who killed him! Good heavens! Could they convict him in the valet’s place, with nobody to speak up for him? They haven’t bothered the valet at all, have they?”

“They questioned him hard,” Alyosha said thoughtfully, “but everyone came to the conclusion that it wasn’t him. He’s lying very sick now. He’s been ill ever since that fit. Really ill,” Alyosha added.
“Oh, dear! Couldn’t you go to that lawyer yourself and tell him the whole thing? They say he was brought down from Petersburg for three thousand roubles.”

“The three thousand came from the three of us together—Ivan, Katerina Ivanovna and me—but she paid the two thousand for the Moscow doctor herself. Fetyukovitch would have charged more, but the case is known all over Russia now. It’s discussed in every paper and journal. Fetyukovitch agreed to come mostly for the glory of it, since the case has become so notorious. I saw him yesterday.”
“Well? Did you speak to him?” Grushenka put in eagerly.
“He listened and said nothing. He told me he had already made up his mind. But he promised to give what I said some thought.”
“Some thought! Ah, they’re swindlers! They’ll be the ruin of him. And why did she send for the doctor?”
“As an expert witness. They want to prove that Mitya is insane and that he committed the murder without knowing what he was doing.” Alyosha smiled gently. “But Mitya won’t agree to that.”

“Yes, but it would be the truth, if he had killed him!” cried Grushenka. “He was mad then, completely mad, and that was my fault, wretch that I am! But of course he didn’t do it, he didn’t do it! And they’re all against him, the whole town. Even Fenya’s testimony went to show he’d done it. And the people at the shop, and that official, and at the tavern earlier, people heard him say it! They’re all, all against him, all shouting against him.”
“Yes, the evidence piles up terribly,” Alyosha remarked grimly.
“And Grigory—Grigory Vassilyevitch—sticks to his story that the door was open. He swears he saw it, and nothing will shake him. I went and talked to him myself. He was rude about it, too.”
“Yes, that may be the strongest evidence against him,” said Alyosha.

“And as for Mitya being mad, he certainly seems so now,” Grushenka began, looking oddly anxious and secretive. “Do you know, Alyosha, I’ve wanted to talk to you about this for ages. I go to see him every day and I’m just amazed by him. Tell me, what do you suppose he’s forever talking about? He goes on and on, and I can’t make anything of it. I thought it was something learned that I was too foolish to follow. Only then he suddenly started on about a babe—some child, that is. ‘Why is the babe poor?’ he said. ‘It’s for that babe that I’m going to Siberia now. I’m not a murderer, but I have to go to Siberia!’ What that meant, what babe, I couldn’t tell you for the life of me. I only cried when he said it, because he said it so sweetly. He cried himself, and I cried too. Then he suddenly kissed me and made the sign of the cross over me. What did it mean, Alyosha? Tell me. What is this babe?”
“It must be Rakitin, who’s been visiting him lately,” Alyosha said, smiling, “though ... this isn’t Rakitin’s doing. I didn’t see Mitya yesterday. I’ll see him today.”

“No, it isn’t Rakitin. It’s his brother, Ivan Fyodorovitch, who’s upsetting him. It’s his visits that do it, that’s what it is,” Grushenka began, and then stopped short. Alyosha stared at her in astonishment.
“Ivan visits him? Has he been there? Mitya told me himself that Ivan hasn’t come once.”

“There ... there! What a girl I am! Letting things slip!” cried Grushenka, flustered, blushing all at once. “Wait, Alyosha, hush! Since I’ve said this much, I’ll tell you the whole truth. He’s been to see him twice. The first time was the moment he arrived. He raced here from Moscow straight away, of course, before I got sick. The second time was a week ago. He told Mitya not to tell you about it, whatever happened, and not to tell anyone at all, really. He came in secret.”
Alyosha sat deep in thought, weighing something. The news had plainly made an impression on him.

“Ivan doesn’t talk to me about Mitya’s case,” he said slowly. “He’s hardly said a word to me these last two months. And every time I go to see him, he seems irritated that I’ve come, so I haven’t been near him for three weeks. H’m!... if he was there a week ago ... then there certainly has been a change in Mitya this week.”

“There has been a change,” Grushenka agreed quickly. “They’ve got a secret, they’ve got a secret! Mitya told me himself that there was a secret, and such a secret that Mitya can’t rest. Before that he was cheerful—and he is cheerful now, for that matter—but when he shakes his head like that, you know, and paces the room and keeps tugging at the hair on his right temple with his right hand, then I know something’s weighing on his mind.... I know! He was cheerful before, though, and he’s cheerful today, too.”
“But you just said he was worried.”

“Yes, he’s worried and cheerful both. One minute he’s irritable, then cheerful, then irritable again. And you know, Alyosha, I’m always amazed at him. With this terrible thing hanging over his head, he sometimes laughs at the most trifling things, like a baby himself.”
“And did he really tell you not to mention Ivan to me? Did he say, ‘Don’t tell him’?”

“Yes, he told me, ‘Don’t tell him.’ It’s you Mitya’s most afraid of. Because it’s a secret, and he said so himself. Alyosha, darling, go to him, find out what their secret is, and come and tell me,” Grushenka begged, suddenly eager. “Set my mind at rest, so I can know the worst that’s coming to me. That’s why I sent for you.”
“You think it concerns you? If it did, he wouldn’t have told you there was a secret.”
“I don’t know. Maybe he wants to tell me and doesn’t dare. He’s giving me a warning. There’s a secret, he says, but he won’t tell me what it is.”
“And what do you think?”

“What do I think? That it’s all over for me, that’s what. The three of them have been plotting to finish me, because Katerina’s part of it. It’s all Katerina, it all comes from her. She’s this and she’s that, which means I’m not. He tells me so in advance, to warn me. He plans to throw me over, that’s the whole secret. They’ve planned it together, the three of them—Mitya, Katerina and Ivan Fyodorovitch. Alyosha, I’ve wanted to ask you for ages. A week ago he suddenly told me that Ivan was in love with Katerina, because he goes to see her so often. Did he tell me the truth or not? Tell me, on your conscience, tell me the worst.”
“I won’t tell you a lie. I don’t think Ivan is in love with Katerina Ivanovna.”

“Oh, that’s what I thought! He’s lying to me, the shameless cheat, that’s all it is! And he was jealous of me just now so that he could put the blame on me afterward. He’s stupid, he can’t hide what he’s up to. He’s so open, you know.... But I’ll pay him back, I’ll pay him back! ‘You believe I did it,’ he said. He said that to me, to me. He threw that in my face! God forgive him! Just wait, I’ll make things hot for Katerina at the trial! I’ll say one little word then ... I’ll tell everything then!”
And she burst into bitter tears again.

“Here’s what I can tell you for certain, Grushenka,” said Alyosha, rising. “First, he loves you. He loves you more than anyone in the world, and you alone, believe me. I know. I do know. Second, I don’t want to pry his secret out of him. But if he tells me of his own accord today, I’ll say straight out that I’ve promised to tell you. Then I’ll come to you today and tell you. Only ... I think ... Katerina Ivanovna has nothing to do with it, and the secret is about something else. That’s certain. It doesn’t seem likely to me that it’s about Katerina Ivanovna. Goodbye for now.”

Alyosha shook her hand. Grushenka was still crying. He could see she put little faith in his comfort, but having had her cry and spoken of her trouble, she was the better for it. He was sorry to leave her in such a state, but he was pressed for time. He still had a great deal to do.
